name: Attention
description: Absinthe, gin, violet and dry vermouth in equal parts. Pale lilac, and considerably stranger than it looks.
funFact: The Savoy prints a whole run of equal-parts absinthe cocktails from the years just after it came back to European bars, and this is the prettiest of them.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Bennett
description: A Gimlet with bitters in it. That one addition changes the whole balance of the drink.
funFact: Two dashes of Angostura is the entire difference between this and a Gin Rickey served up, which is a fair summary of how the old books drew their distinctions.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Colony
description: Gin, grapefruit and maraschino. Named for the Manhattan restaurant where being seated badly was a public event.
funFact: The Colony's headwaiter Gene Cavallero was famous for seating people by status rather than reservation, which made the front room the most contested real estate in the city.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Commodore
description: Rye with lemon, grenadine and orange bitters. A sour with a red tint and a dry finish.
funFact: Real grenadine is pomegranate syrup, not red sugar water, and in a drink this simple the difference between the two is the whole drink.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.

name: Duchess
description: Absinthe with both vermouths, in thirds. No base spirit at all — the absinthe is the base.
funFact: Absinthe was banned across most of Europe and America when this was written down, which is exactly why the drinks that used it read as daring rather than quaint.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.

name: Earthquake
description: Gin, whisky and absinthe in equal measure. The name is a warning, not a flourish.
funFact: Toulouse-Lautrec drank a version of this made from cognac and absinthe and called it tremblement de terre, which the London version borrowed and then made worse.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.

Strain into a chilled glass.

name: Fourth Degree
description: Gin with both vermouths and a rinse of absinthe. A Perfect Martini with the corners taken off.
funFact: Splitting the vermouth between dry and sweet is what bartenders call perfect, a term that predates the Martini and applies to any drink built this way.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.

name: Gin and It
description: Gin and Italian vermouth, at room temperature and without ice. The Martini before refrigeration reached the bar.
funFact: It is served warm on purpose — the drink dates from London bars that had no reliable ice, and chilling it turns it into something else entirely.

steps: Pour the gin and the sweet vermouth straight into a small glass.
Stir them together briefly with a barspoon.
Add no ice and do not chill the glass.
Drop in a cherry and serve.

name: Grand Slam
description: Swedish punsch with both vermouths. Sweet, spiced and almost entirely forgotten.
funFact: Swedish punsch is built on Batavian arrack shipped from Java, which is how an Indonesian spirit ended up defining a Scandinavian liqueur.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.

Strain into a chilled glass.

name: Hoop La
description: Equal parts Lillet, Cointreau, brandy and lemon. A Corpse Reviver with brandy where the gin should be.
funFact: It shares its skeleton exactly with the Corpse Reviver No. 2 — four equal parts, one of them citrus — which is the most reliable template in the whole Savoy book.

name: Maiden's Blush
description: Gin with curaçao, grenadine and lemon. Named for its colour, which is the palest possible pink.
funFact: The Savoy prints two different drinks under this name, one with curaçao and one with absinthe, and gives no hint as to which came first.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.

name: Moonlight
description: Kirsch, grapefruit and sugar. Three ingredients, dry as a bone, and nothing like as sweet as cherry brandy suggests.
funFact: Kirsch is distilled with the cherry stones left in, which is where its faint bitter-almond edge comes from and why it is not a sweet liqueur.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.

name: Nineteen Twenty
description: Kirsch, gin and sweet vermouth in thirds. A Martini with cherry stones running through it.
funFact: Drinks named for years cluster around 1920 in the old books, and almost all of them were invented in Europe by American bartenders who had just left home.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.

name: Prince of Wales
description: Rye, maraschino and pineapple under champagne, and attributed to a king who liked his drinks complicated.
funFact: The recipe is credited to Edward VII from his years as Prince of Wales, a period he spent building a reputation that made the attribution entirely plausible.

steps: Muddle the pineapple with the maraschino and bitters in a shaker.
Add the rye and ice, and shake hard.
Double-strain into a chilled flute.
Top with champagne and add an orange twist.

name: Soul Kiss
description: Dubonnet, dry vermouth, rye and orange juice. Low, aromatic and easier than its name suggests.
funFact: Dubonnet was created in 1846 to make quinine palatable to French soldiers in North Africa, which is a strange origin for something this gentle.

name: Southern Bride
description: Gin, grapefruit and a bar spoon of maraschino. The Colony's shape with the proportions moved.
funFact: Maraschino is measured in barspoons rather than ounces for good reason — it is made from whole crushed Marasca cherries, stones included, and takes over a drink quickly.

name: Whist
description: Applejack, rum and sweet vermouth. Named for the card game bridge was built out of.
funFact: Whist ruled English card tables for two centuries before bridge displaced it, which dates the naming convention as precisely as anything in the book.
